code.note: Build with the autotools files in the archive (libridc from src/, then examples/explicit). run.sh runs the explicit executable at order 4 with nt = 10, 20, 40, 80, 160 and diffs each output against ref/n*.ref; the rerun should use the n1 case only for this claim.

claim.location: Shipped reference output 965/examples/explicit/ref/n1.ref, the first line. explicit.cpp prints sol[i] with %14.12f after running ridc_fe at order 4 with nt = 10 steps on the test system u_i' = -(i+1) t u_i over [0,1] with u_i(0) = 1 (explicit.cpp rhs; run.sh, STEPS=10). The exact first component is exp(-1/2) = 0.6065306597, so the printed value carries the method's own error and is not the closed form. The n1.ref file is the code's own output, not an echo of the input.
claim.paper_value: sol[0] = 0.606521722539 (n1.ref line 1; ./explicit 4 10 prints this as the first line)
claim.metric: first component sol[0] printed by ./explicit 4 10 (order 4, nt 10), compared as a number
claim.determinism: deterministic (fixed ODE, no random input; the driver takes no seed)

tolerance.basis: Fixed before any run. The reference is printed to 12 decimal places, so the rounding step is 1e-12; the shipped driver compares exactly as text. A tolerance of 1e-11 absolute allows the last printed digit to change across compilers and math libraries and nothing larger. The n1 case is a 10-step integration with an order-4 method, so an error above 1e-11 would be a real change in the code's output, not rounding. Not to be loosened after any run.

cost.cpu_minutes_estimate: Under 1 minute: one 10-step run of a 2-equation ODE.
cost.data_size: None: the driver generates its own initial condition.
cost.data_licence: No data. Code licence is not stated in the archive README; the rerun should record it.

why: The authors' own shipped driver and reference output test a parallel time integrator on a fixed ODE, and the number needs the full RIDC iteration to compute, so it tests the old C++ code on a modern toolchain rather than a closed form.
